advances: The proposed uniform inequality \(\max_j r_A(j)\ge 2|A|/2^n-1\) is false. An explicit full-dimensional lattice tetrahedron has exactly twenty lattice points and maximum oriented, zero-inclusive reflection count three, whereas the proposed lower bound is four. Boolean products give the same obstruction in every ambient dimension at least three and force any absolute constant in the universal lower bound \(\max_jr_B(j)\ge(1+\eta)|B|/2^n\), required whenever \(|B|>2^{n+1}\), to satisfy \(\eta\le1/5\). A vertex-deficit argument proves that twenty is the largest possible cardinality of a full-dimensional three-dimensional lattice-convex set with maximum reflection count at most three. No conclusion is claimed for the existence of a universal \(\eta\in(0,1/5]\).

The lattice census, all-center reflection certificate, product construction, and vertex-deficit inequality are proved with exact finite integer arithmetic and elementary convexity. The declared predecessor is used only for the canonical admissibility and Hellinger normalization.
proof:
The determinant of the three nonzero vertices of \(P\) is \(78\), so \(P\) is a compact full-dimensional lattice tetrahedron. The barycentric coefficients of \((x,y,z)\) with respect to its four vertices in the displayed order are \(1-x-y+83z/78\), \(x-31z/78\), \(y-53z/78\), and \(z/78\). Therefore membership in \(P\) is equivalent to

\(z\ge0\), \(78x\ge31z\), \(78y\ge53z\), and \(78(x+y)\le78+83z\).

The middle two inequalities give \(78(x+y)\ge84z\); together with the last they imply \(z\le78\). At integer height zero the solutions are \((0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\). At height \(78\) the unique solution is \((31,53,78)\).

For an integer height \(1\le z\le77\), the second and third barycentric coefficients are nonnegative and have sum at most \(1-z/78<1\). Thus, if an integer point exists at that height, its first two coordinates are forced to be \(x=\lceil31z/78\rceil\) and \(y=\lceil53z/78\rceil\). Indeed, increasing either coordinate above its ceiling would make its corresponding barycentric coefficient at least one. Conversely, this forced point belongs to \(P\) if and only if

\(s_z:=78+83z-78\lceil31z/78\rceil-78\lceil53z/78\rceil\ge0\).

The following are all seventy-seven integer slacks, with each row listing consecutive heights in increasing order. Each entry uses only \(\lceil az/78\rceil=\lfloor(az+77)/78\rfloor\).

```text
heights       s_z, in increasing height order
 1 through 11:    5,  10, -63,  20,  25, -48,  35, -38, -33,  50, -23
12 through 22:  -18, -13,  -8,  -3,   2,   7, -66,  17,  22, -51,  32
23 through 33:  -41, -36,  47, -26, -21, -94, -11,  -6, -79,   4, -69
34 through 44:  -64,  19, -54, -49, -44, -39, -34, -29, -24, -97, -14
45 through 55:   -9, -82,   1, -72, -67,  16, -57, -52,-125, -42, -37
56 through 66: -110, -27,-100, -95, -12, -85, -80, -75, -70, -65, -60
67 through 77:  -55,-128, -45, -40,-113, -30,-103, -98, -15, -88, -83
```

Precisely the heights \(1,2,4,5,7,10,16,17,19,20,22,25,32,35,47,50\) have nonnegative slack. Together with the endpoint heights this proves the following complete lattice census; the indices will also give the reflection certificate.

```text
 i       p_i                 i       p_i
 0     ( 0, 0, 0)           10     ( 7,12,17)
 1     ( 1, 0, 0)           11     ( 8,13,19)
 2     ( 0, 1, 0)           12     ( 8,14,20)
 3     ( 1, 1, 1)           13     ( 9,15,22)
 4     ( 1, 2, 2)           14     (10,17,25)
 5     ( 2, 3, 4)           15     (13,22,32)
 6     ( 2, 4, 5)           16     (14,24,35)
 7     ( 3, 5, 7)           17     (19,32,47)
 8     ( 4, 7,10)           18     (20,34,50)
 9     ( 7,11,16)           19     (31,53,78)
```

In particular \(A=\{p_0,\ldots,p_{19}\}\). Since \(A\subseteq P\) and contains all vertices of \(P\), its convex hull is exactly \(P\); the lattice-convexity equality \(A=\operatorname{conv}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^3\) follows. All sixteen intermediate points are interior: their slacks in the table are positive, their heights lie strictly between zero and \(78\), and both \(31\) and \(53\) are coprime to \(78\), so their second and third barycentric coefficients are strictly positive.

Here is an exhaustive reflection check. The parity classes, expressed by indices in this census, are

```text
parity       indices
000          0,12,18
001          6,16
010          2,5,8
011          11,14
100          1,4,15
101          10,17
110          9,13,19
111          3,7
```

Two integer endpoints have an integer midpoint if and only if their parity vectors agree. The four classes of size three provide three unordered distinct pairs each, and the four classes of size two provide one each. Thus there are exactly sixteen unordered distinct pairs with integer centers. The next table lists all sixteen, with \(p_i+p_k=2p_j\) in every row.

```text
center j    endpoint indices (i,k)      center j    endpoint indices (i,k)
   3                (1,4)                 11                (9,13)
   4                (2,5)                 12                (6,16)
   5                (3,7)                 13               (11,14)
   6                (2,8)                 14                (0,18)
   7                (5,8)                 15               (10,17)
   8               (0,12)                 16               (12,18)
   9               (1,15)                 17                (9,19)
  10               (4,15)                 18               (13,19)
```

The endpoint pairs in this table are exactly all pairs allowed by the parity table, and their center indices are exactly \(3,4,\ldots,18\), each once. Therefore each of these sixteen centers has two nonzero oriented displacements and one zero displacement, giving reflection count three. The other four supported centers have no distinct pair and have reflection count one. If an integer point \(j\) outside \(A\) had a reflected endpoint pair in \(A\), then \(j\) would be their midpoint and hence would belong to \(P\cap\mathbb Z^3=A\), a contradiction. This proves the asserted counts at every integer center.

Both finite certificates were also checked in a second direct form: the bounding box \(0\le x\le31\), \(0\le y\le53\), \(0\le z\le78\) contains \(P\), and testing its \(136512\) integer points against the four integer inequalities above gives exactly the displayed twenty points. For each of those twenty centers, counting \(x\in A\) such that \(2j-x\in A\) gives one at indices \(0,1,2,19\) and three at all other indices. These checks use exact integer arithmetic. The complete slack, parity, and endpoint tables above supply the arithmetic certificate without requiring an external script.

For the higher-dimensional examples, the convex hull of \(A\times\{0,1\}^{n-3}\) is \(P\times[0,1]^{n-3}\). To verify the nontrivial containment, a convex representation of a point of \(P\) by points of \(A\), and a convex representation of a point of the cube by Boolean vertices, combine by multiplying their coefficients. The product hull is full-dimensional, and its integer points are exactly the asserted product support. At a supported center, an integer displacement in a Boolean coordinate must be zero, because both reflected endpoints must lie in \(\{0,1\}\). Thus its reflection count is precisely the count at its first three coordinates, with maximum three. A center outside the product support again has count zero by lattice-convexity. Its cardinality is \(20\cdot2^{n-3}\), so its cardinality divided by \(2^n\) is \(5/2>2\). It is therefore a nonempty finite lattice-convex set in an integer dimension \(n\ge3\ge1\) satisfying the strict hypothesis \(|B|>2^{n+1}\) of the universal separation assertion, with \(B=A\times\{0,1\}^{n-3}\). Its reflection ratio is \(3/(5/2)=6/5\). For every fixed real \(\eta>1/5\), the proposed lower bound at this support is \((1+\eta)|B|/2^n=(1+\eta)(5/2)>3=\max_{j\in\mathbb Z^n}r_B(j)\). Thus every \(\eta>1/5\) is excluded, in every dimension \(n\ge3\), and any constant satisfying the universal assertion must obey \(\eta\le1/5\).

For the Hellinger normalization, take \(w\) to be the indicator of the product support and extend it by the indicator of \(P\times[0,1]^{n-3}\). This finite-valued extension agrees at every lattice point, including every zero. It is globally log-concave: if both endpoint values are one their connecting segment lies in the convex set; if either value is zero the required right side is zero. Hence it satisfies the exact admissibility hypothesis of accepted fact ab57fac07c0d3160. The indicator weights give \(M=1\), \(W=20\cdot2^{n-3}\), and \(H_j=r(j)\), so \(H_*=3\), \(G=\log(6/5)\), and \(\rho=2/5\).

It remains to prove the asserted extremality bound. Put \(N=|B|\), and let \(N_b\) be its cardinalities in the \(2^n\) ambient parity classes, allowing empty classes. The bijection \((x,y)\mapsto((x+y)/2,(x-y)/2)\) between ordered same-parity endpoint pairs and integer-centered reflected pairs, together with lattice-convexity, gives \(\sum_bN_b^2=\sum_{j\in B}r_B(j)\). At every vertex the count is one: an extreme point cannot be the midpoint of two distinct points of its convex hull. At every other point it is at most three. Consequently \(\sum_bN_b^2\le3N-2v_B\).

For every nonnegative integer \(m\), the two consecutive integers \(m-2\) and \(m-3\) have nonnegative product. Thus \(m^2\ge5m-6\), and summing this inequality over the ambient parity classes gives \(\sum_bN_b^2\ge5N-6\cdot2^n\). Combining the two bounds yields \(N\le3\cdot2^n-v_B\). A full-dimensional convex hull in \(\mathbb R^3\) has at least four vertices, so \(N\le24-4=20\), attained by the displayed example.

This last argument only gives \(|B|\le3\cdot2^n-(n+1)\) for full-dimensional sets in growing dimension. Therefore it does not supply a positive absolute gap between \(3\) and \(|B|/2^n\). The explicit family proved here keeps that latter ratio at \(5/2\), and does not resolve whether there exists an absolute \(\eta\in(0,1/5]\) for which the universal reflection inequality stated above holds for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every nonempty finite lattice-convex \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) with \(|B|>2^{n+1}\).
statement:
For every integer \(n\ge1\) and every nonempty finite lattice-convex set \(A\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), write \(r_A(j)=|\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:j+v,j-v\in A\}|\), for \(j\in\mathbb Z^n\). Displacements are oriented and zero is included exactly once at every center in \(A\).

The weaker separation assertion asks whether there exists an absolute real constant \(\eta>0\), independent of the dimension and the support, such that for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every nonempty finite set \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) satisfying \(B=\operatorname{conv}(B)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) and \(|B|>2^{n+1}\), one has \(\max_{j\in\mathbb Z^n}r_B(j)\ge(1+\eta)|B|/2^n\). No full-dimensionality assumption is imposed on \(B\). Here \(r_B\) uses exactly the reflection definition above with \(A=B\). The counterexamples below exclude every real \(\eta>1/5\) for this universal assertion.

Let

\(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(31,53,78)\}\subset\mathbb R^3\), and let \(A=P\cap\mathbb Z^3\).

Then \(P\) is full-dimensional, \(|A|=20\), and \(\max_{j\in\mathbb Z^3}r_A(j)=3\). More precisely, the four vertices of \(P\) have reflection count one, its sixteen other lattice points have reflection count three, and every integer center outside \(P\) has reflection count zero. Thus \(3<2\cdot20/2^3-1=4\).

For every integer \(n\ge3\), the set \(A\times\{0,1\}^{n-3}\) is full-dimensional and lattice-convex in \(\mathbb Z^n\), has \(20\cdot2^{n-3}>2^{n+1}\) points, and has maximum reflection count three. Its ratio \(\max_jr(j)/(|A\times\{0,1\}^{n-3}|/2^n)\) is exactly \(6/5\). These examples meet the strict cardinality hypothesis of the universal separation assertion. For every real \(\eta>1/5\), they violate its inequality, since \(3<(1+\eta)(5/2)\). Consequently no such \(\eta\) can satisfy that assertion.

Use the canonical Hellinger quantities of accepted fact ab57fac07c0d3160: \(W=\sum_z w_z\), \(M=\max_z w_z\), \(H_j=\sum_v\sqrt{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}\), \(H_*=\max_jH_j\), \(G=\log(2^nH_*/W)\), and \(\rho=2^nM/W\). For the indicator table of each of these product supports, the table is admissible with all zero lattice values preserved, and \(G=\log(6/5)\), \(\rho=2/5\). These fixed positive-gain examples do not give a sequence with \(G\to0\).

Finally, if \(B\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is any nonempty finite lattice-convex set with \(\max_jr_B(j)\le3\), and its convex hull has \(v_B\) vertices, then \(|B|\le3\cdot2^n-v_B\). In particular, a full-dimensional such set in \(\mathbb Z^3\) has at most twenty points, and the displayed tetrahedron attains this maximum. The exponent \(n\) in this assertion is the ambient lattice dimension; no substitution of affine rank is implicit.
